title: The Decision to Turn South
subtitle: The competing plans and the conditions beneath them
author: Robert M. Dobo
phase: II — The Drive into the Soviet Interior
summary: Hitler’s decision of 21 August redirected German effort towards Ukraine. Comparing it with the conditional Moscow proposal, Soviet warnings and Order No. 270 restores the uncertainty and coercion within which the next operations began.
body:
Hitler’s written decision of 21 August 1941 put Ukraine ahead of an immediate assault on Moscow. Destroying Soviet forces in the south, securing the Donets industrial region, taking the Crimea and interrupting oil supplies from the Caucasus received priority. Leningrad and contact with Finland remained objectives in the north. The decision was consequential, but it was not a choice between an available victory and an inexplicable diversion. The alternative submitted three days earlier also required repair, concentration and the successful conclusion of battles still in progress. [1] The dispute concerned how another operation might finally break Soviet resistance. Army leaders favoured concentrating against the forces before Moscow; Hitler placed greater weight on the southern enemy grouping and the resources sustaining the Soviet war effort. Both arguments depended on assumptions about what the German army could still accomplish and what losses the Soviet state could survive. The dated proposals make those assumptions visible. They also prevent the later catastrophe at Kiev from being treated as an outcome already achieved—or inevitable—when the decision was made.

The Moscow proposal and its conditions

The immediate alternative to Hitler’s decision was developed in the German Army High Command’s memorandum of 18 August. It argued that the main surviving Soviet strength stood before Moscow and that a concentrated offensive there offered the best chance of decisive destruction. The capital’s importance as a political centre and communications hub reinforced this operational argument. Nevertheless, the memorandum was a plan for an offensive after preparation, rather than evidence that a fully supplied army could simply resume the advance that afternoon. Its timetable and force allocations reveal how much remained to be accomplished. [1] The proposed southern assault group was particularly substantial: twelve infantry divisions and six armoured or motorised divisions would attack on an approximately eighty-mile front between the Bryansk and Roslavl areas toward Kaluga. Farther north, separate groupings would move through the approaches to Bely and Rzhev. Ten infantry divisions would hold the broad intervening sector east of Smolensk. This was an attempt to turn a geographically dispersed army group into converging assault forces. It required assembly, coordination and the protection of the intervening front, not merely the selection of a direction on a map. [1] The timetable also depended on battles outside the proposed main axis. The fighting around Gomel was supposed to be successfully concluded by 23 August. An operation around Velikiye Luki was to begin on the twenty-first. Repairs were expected to make the mobile formations available toward the end of the month, with the main offensive possible early in September. Each condition could affect the others. A division held near Gomel could not simultaneously assemble for an attack toward Kaluga; a vehicle waiting for an engine could not transport ammunition simply because its formation had been assigned a new objective. [1] The memorandum’s conditions are part of the proposal, not qualifications to be discarded when judging it. Its advocates expected other battles to finish, repaired formations to become available and a broad front to remain protected during concentration. If those assumptions held, they believed a major operation towards Moscow could begin in early September. Their confidence deserves examination; it is not evidence that the conditions had already been met. Nor does the plan establish that taking the capital would have ended Soviet resistance. That further claim requires an argument the proposed axis of advance cannot supply on its own. [1]

The southern flank as an operational problem

The southern alternative grew from the relationship between Army Groups Centre and South. As Centre advanced eastward through Belarus, its right flank extended beyond the forces operating in Ukraine. Soviet formations around Gomel and farther south could threaten the communications behind the advancing German armies. Their continued presence also obstructed a direct connection between the two army groups. The issue was therefore both defensive and offensive: securing German communications might create the opportunity to strike behind the Soviet armies defending the Dnieper and Kiev. [2] The Soviet 5th Army was central to this calculation. Operating north and northwest of Kiev, it had complicated Army Group South’s progress while remaining vulnerable to a movement descending from the north. Hitler’s instructions sought a concentric operation by the adjoining wings of the two army groups to prevent Soviet forces escaping eastward. Army Group Centre was to provide the forces necessary for that task even if doing so delayed a subsequent operation elsewhere. This requirement changed the scale of the commitment: the southward movement became an operational priority in its own right. [1] Gomel’s fall did not eliminate the work between decision and execution. As the preceding study showed, Soviet troops were still fighting east of the city and around the Sozh and Iput crossings after German forces entered it. For Weichs’s 2nd Army and Guderian’s 2nd Panzer Group, moving farther south meant crossing additional rivers, controlling junctions and securing the routes behind the leading formations. The infantry army’s position and the panzer group’s movements had to be related to each other, even though their speeds and supply requirements differed. [3] The Moscow plan itself provided for a substantial covering force east of Gomel and troops in the Pripyat region. Both proposals therefore addressed the southern flank, but assigned different scales and purposes to the response. A limited securing operation aimed to protect the central offensive while preserving its main concentration. A deeper movement towards the rear of Kiev sought a major result in the south and accepted delay elsewhere. The disagreement concerned the force required, the risk that could be tolerated and the value of the expected outcome. Those distinctions make the alternatives more precise than a choice between recognising and ignoring the flank. [1]

Time in the strategic calculation

A staff officer’s calendar

Blau’s reconstruction records Warlimont’s 18 August estimate that roughly eight weeks remained for northern operations and thirteen for those in the south before winter. The figures supported his recommendation to concentrate on Moscow, even if some flank and rear dangers had to be accepted. They were planning judgements about a shrinking interval, rather than forecasts of conditions on every road. The estimate reveals how advocates of the central offensive framed the opportunity cost of diversion: time spent elsewhere could consume the period in which their preferred operation remained practicable. It does not establish that the risks they proposed accepting would have remained manageable.

[1]

Resources, objectives and the enemy still in the field

Hitler’s reply incorporated a different conception of how the Soviet Union could be defeated. The Donets basin offered an industrial target, the Crimea threatened the security of the Romanian oil region through Soviet air operations, and a further movement toward the Caucasus promised pressure on Soviet oil supplies. These objectives joined military geography to the economic foundations of the war. They also extended the scale of the undertaking. Destroying an army west of the Dnieper, occupying an industrial region and cutting a distant petroleum supply were connected ambitions, but success in one did not automatically accomplish the others. [1] Hitler’s concern for the Crimea connected the southern operation to Romania’s importance as a source of petroleum. Soviet aircraft operating from the peninsula presented a threat to those oilfields in his assessment, giving its capture a place within Germany’s wider war economy. Translating that priority into conquest would require a distinct commitment of troops, engineering and supply. The strategic problem was consequently one of sequence as well as purpose: protecting a valuable resource could draw forces into an operation whose demands competed with those of destroying Soviet armies elsewhere. The economic argument identified a reason to act without resolving the means or timing. [1] The northern priority imposed another competing demand. Leningrad was to be isolated and contact established with Finnish forces. German plans also linked the eventual Moscow offensive to the release of formations and air support from the northern operation. This interdependence made the apparent sequence fragile. If the north required longer than expected, forces promised for the centre would remain unavailable; if Soviet counterattacks forced additional German reinforcement, the sequence could become a further redistribution. The directive of 21 August expressed a hierarchy of objectives, but it could not guarantee that the enemy would permit them to be completed in that order. [1] The rival proposals also defined the mechanism of decision differently. Army leaders placed greater emphasis on destroying the forces believed to be concentrated before Moscow. Hitler joined destruction in Ukraine to the seizure or denial of resources supporting Soviet resistance. Both required assumptions about how military loss would affect the state’s ability to continue. Earlier encirclements had not prevented new armies from appearing, and occupation of industrial territory could yield less usable production if machinery had been removed or destroyed. The planners therefore had to connect the immediate operation to a wider process of collapse whose conditions their victories had yet to establish. [1]

Guderian and the movement that followed

The southern operation substituted a different set of demands. Connections between Centre and South had to be established across the operational space still occupied by Soviet troops. Bridges and roads had to remain usable after the assault formations passed, and forces guarding them needed supplies as well. The likely gain was a more secure junction between army groups and the destruction of an enemy concentration. The immediate price was additional movement and another period in which workshops and transport columns had to support formations operating farther from their previous assembly areas. This was a resource allocation decision within an already active campaign. [1] Guderian’s role needs to be placed within this sequence rather than made its sole explanation. His 2nd Panzer Group supplied the principal mobile instrument for the southward operation. On 23 August, after the written decision had been issued, he met Hitler in an attempt to reopen the argument. Halder and Bock hoped that the commander’s direct account of his troops and their prospects might support a renewed concentration toward Moscow. The attempt failed to reverse the decision. The date matters: the meeting was a subsequent effort to alter an established priority, not the occasion on which the original written order was issued. [2] The resulting movement did not carry every formation associated with Guderian in a single intact block. The operational account records that much of his infantry and a panzer corps remained to protect the flank under Kluge’s 4th Army while the striking force moved south. Such allocations expose the cost of changing direction. A headquarters could receive a large objective while its immediately available force was reduced by the obligation to cover the space it had already crossed. Mobile warfare produced vulnerable communications as well as opportunities for further penetration. [2] By 25 August, the German 2nd Army and 2nd Panzer Group were beginning the larger southward operation. Their movement would develop toward the routes behind the Soviet Southwestern Front, with the panzer group eventually driving toward Romny. That destination describes the developing operation; it should not be placed under German control on 21 August. Nor should the later junction with forces advancing north from Army Group South be treated as an accomplished fact at the moment of decision. The September encirclement required additional advances, crossings and Soviet decisions that still lay ahead. [2] The division of Guderian’s forces also limits the image of a whole army group simply pivoting south. Units retained on the old flank continued to serve the new operation by protecting its connection to the centre. They were simultaneously unavailable for its leading attack. German command thus accepted a specific distribution of risk: enough force would remain to hold the central position while the principal mobile effort sought a larger result in Ukraine. Soviet attacks around Smolensk continued to test that calculation. [1]

What Moscow understood, and what Kiev was ordered to hold

Soviet command was not wholly unaware of the southern danger. On 19 August, Shaposhnikov informed Zhukov that he and Stalin accepted the likelihood of a German movement southward. The Southwestern Direction and the fronts concerned were warned, while instructions continued to insist on holding Kiev and the Dnieper line. This combination is more revealing than a simple claim that Stalin either knew nothing or knew everything. The warning identified a possible enemy intention; it did not settle how much ground should be abandoned, how quickly an army could withdraw or which danger deserved immediate priority. [2] The Soviet command also took measures to protect the threatened junction. The Bryansk Front had been established under Andrei Eremenko during the middle of August, initially with the danger to the Moscow direction prominent in its responsibilities. As German forces turned south, the relationship between that front and the neighbouring armies became increasingly important. A new front headquarters could concentrate responsibility and coordinate reserves, but its existence did not itself provide the trained troops, communications or freedom of movement required to stop a panzer group. Organisational adaptation and operational capability developed on different schedules. [2] There were also authorised withdrawals. The Southwestern Direction’s order of 19 August instructed the 5th Army to begin moving behind the Dnieper during the night of 19–20 August and provided for a northern defensive flank toward the Chernigov area. It specified the use of divisions for that protection and referred to the 293rd Rifle Division arriving by rail near Sumy. These were concrete attempts to reposition forces while preserving the larger defence. Their limitations became apparent when the enemy threatened routes farther east than the line the army had been ordered to occupy. [4] Retaining Kiev preserved a defended crossing region within the Dnieper position, but its value depended on the communications of the armies around it remaining usable. A penetration descending farther east could change that calculation before troops defending the city experienced an immediate tactical defeat. The Soviet command’s problem therefore lay in converting recognition of a possible threat into timely authority for an adequate response. Warnings and local withdrawals demonstrate awareness, while continued instructions to hold show the limits imposed on action. Their interaction explains the developing danger more accurately than a claim that knowledge alone would have prevented it. [2] At this endpoint, the warning had not produced a settled answer about the timing or extent of further withdrawal. Later knowledge of the encirclement cannot be assigned to every officer making decisions in August. The evidence nevertheless establishes that the southern danger had been identified before the German written decision of 21 August.

The command climate and the people beneath it

Order No. 270, issued on 16 August, formed part of the coercive setting in which Soviet commanders and soldiers faced these decisions. It instructed encircled formations to continue fighting and break through to their own troops. At the same time, it treated surrender and desertion through sweeping accusations against named officers and threatened severe punishment. Commanders and political officers classed as malicious deserters were to be shot, and their families arrested. Families of ordinary soldiers who surrendered were to lose state assistance. These were explicit measures of collective punishment, not simply appeals for military determination. [5] The order accused Ponedelin and Kirillov of desertion and surrender at Uman, using their supposed conduct as a warning to others. The [Uman study](/articles/barbarossa-the-uman-encirclement-1941-08-06) follows the surviving requests for aid and attempts to break out. Those documents do not settle every command decision, but they prevent the punitive order from serving as an uncontested narrative of the defeat. Order No. 270 was designed to compel conduct by praise, accusation and threat. Its assertion that escape had been available to a named officer needs evidence beyond the assertion itself. A commander’s capture establishes captivity; it does not independently establish cowardice or willing collaboration. [5] For civilian households, the same policy extended military events into the conditions of survival at home. A soldier’s capture could threaten a family’s material support; an officer’s classification could expose relatives to arrest. The threatened penalties were especially consequential in a war already disrupting wages, housing and access to food. The state demanded continued resistance while making families answerable for actions they could neither observe nor control. This aspect of Soviet policy belongs in the history of the battlefield because it shaped the consequences of defeat beyond the men physically present in an encirclement. [5] The order also called on encircled troops to resist superiors who proposed surrender, authorising their destruction rather than obedience. In another provision, division commanders and commissars were to remove battalion and regimental commanders accused of hiding from battle, demote them and, if considered necessary, shoot them on the spot. The text therefore demanded both obedience in combat and violent action against officers classified as failing that duty. It records authorised coercion, not the frequency with which these punishments were carried out. Its circulation to companies, squadrons, batteries and headquarters was intended to make that threat widely known. The resulting command climate belongs in the analysis without turning every withdrawal into disobedience or every act of endurance into proof of political enthusiasm.[5] German plans exposed civilians to a different, separately documented threat. The supplement to Directive No. 34, issued on 12 August, had halted a direct assault on Kiev while envisaging the city’s destruction by incendiary bombing and artillery when the necessary means became available. This was an intention in an operational directive, not evidence that the contemplated destruction had already occurred. Nevertheless, it shows how the civilian city entered German planning as a target to be devastated rather than merely a position to be bypassed. The distinction between military manoeuvre and violence against urban life was already breaking down within the instructions themselves. [1]

Schoolbooks on an evacuation train

Agnessa Margolina recalled leaving Kiev with relatives in August 1941. In her 2003 interview for Centropa, she described carrying her four-year-old cousin Boris while her stepmother carried a suitcase. Her brothers brought textbooks for the next school year. The family travelled independently of a workplace evacuation, boarding a crowded freight train fitted with plank sleeping platforms. Her account remembers bombing, interruptions and uncertainty about the destination.

The interview does not establish an exact departure day, and some of its later dates and geographical details are inconsistent. Its account of the family’s luggage should therefore remain an attributed recollection. The schoolbooks nevertheless illuminate a recognisably different scale of planning from that of the headquarters: children preparing to continue an interrupted education while adults tried to move a multigenerational household beyond the fighting. Their escape depended on the same railway capacity that the armies and evacuated factories also required. [6]

An expanding war economy

The strategic argument in Germany coincided with a different discussion about resources among the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States. On 18 August, the State Department transmitted the signed Roosevelt–Churchill message proposing a conference in Moscow to consider future assistance. The message explicitly described a long struggle and acknowledged that even substantial British and American resources were limited. Allocation required decisions about competing fronts, manufactured equipment and raw materials. Its significance lay in the attempt to organise sustained cooperation, rather than in any immediate transformation of Soviet combat strength. [7] The joint message distinguished immediate deliveries from a longer programme to be negotiated. That distinction prevents aid from becoming an abstract counterweight to German territorial gains. Equipment already shipped, equipment promised and equipment available to a Soviet formation were different quantities. Yet the longer programme mattered because it offered a way to sustain resistance beyond the campaign Germany had expected to decide quickly. The German and Allied arguments about resources were therefore connected, while operating on timetables that could not be collapsed into a single balance for August. [7] The relationship between these economic strategies makes the Moscow counterfactual difficult to resolve with confidence. David Stahel argues that German losses, overextension and Soviet endurance had already undermined the campaign’s original assumptions, and he challenges a narrative in which an otherwise attainable victory was lost through one diversion. His introduction to Kiev 1941 also emphasises the influence of German postwar memoirs on that interpretation. This does not make every alternative equally plausible or remove the costs of the southward operation. It does require the historian to examine what the army could sustain, what the enemy could still do and how much a captured objective would actually change. [8] The alternative to turning south remains a legitimate historical question. It becomes answerable only when its terms are specified: the proposed forces, the earliest feasible start, the opposition, and the result being claimed. Capturing Moscow, destroying the armies defending it and ending the Soviet Union’s ability to continue were separate propositions. The 18 August memorandum documents a plan for the first stages of such an operation. It cannot prove the final proposition. Rejecting certainty about an unexecuted victory does not require denying the costs of the operation Hitler chose. [1]

A decision whose outcome remained open

On 21 August the priority had changed; the southern result remained to be won. Guderian’s meeting with Hitler on the twenty-third failed to reverse the decision, and the larger movement began on the twenty-fifth. Keeping these dates separate restores the interval between decision and execution. The September encirclement lies beyond it. For now, the German command had committed its mobile strength to another operation while relying on forces left in the centre to contain continuing Soviet pressure. [2] The Soviet command had warnings, a newly created front and orders for limited withdrawal, alongside the continuing requirement to hold Kiev. Its punitive policy extended the consequences of capture into soldiers’ households. These were the conditions in which the next decisions would be taken, not a retrospective verdict on every person caught by them. The [closing study](/articles/barbarossa-a-front-divided-1941-08-25) returns to 25 August to examine the battles still continuing elsewhere and the people whose lives the expanding occupation placed in danger.

sourceMethod: Numbered notes identify the passages used and return from each source entry to its first citation. Russian military documents were consulted in published transcription; English accounts are paraphrases, and printed archival references do not imply direct inspection of originals. Orders establish assigned tasks, while reports preserve contemporary knowledge, claims and omissions. Retrospective German operational accounts are assessed alongside Soviet records and other scholarship. Testimony is attributed and dated separately from the events recalled. Later developments are identified explicitly. This local revision also draws on retained source extracts where a fresh public retrieval was unavailable; the accompanying editorial report records those access limits.
